MDA asset Condition and functionality

At MDA level, apart from sixteen faulty assets at Ministry of Works and Transport, one faulty double-cabin pickup at Ministry of Health and three faulty laptops at the Office of the Prime minister, the rest of the assets, 16,643 (99.9%), were recorded as functional and in use. The Ministry of Education and Sports holds 10,783 of these assets, mainly TELA handsets and tablets, all recorded as in use at the different schools across the country. LGFC and MoPS indicated that they never received UgIFT assets.

4 Asset management
4.1 Maintenance and repairs

Maintenance keeps UgIFT assets working for the services they were bought to support. Most of the verified assets are furniture, clinical equipment and computers in daily use at Health Centres and seed schools, where wear and breakage are to be expected. Routine checks, a record of faults and a dependable route for repair decide whether a broken item returns to use quickly or stays out of service. During the verification, each facility was asked how it maintains, repairs, services or replaces UgIFT assets and whether it keeps a regular record of their functionality or breakdown.

following_text: Figure 46: Most facilities met repairs from their own funds or staff

Frequency. Few facilities worked to a fixed maintenance interval. Of the 494 programme-list facilities that described how they maintain UgIFT assets or check their condition, 50 (10.1%) did so at a fixed interval. Of these 50, 14 (28.0%) worked annually, 11 (22.0%) monthly, 10 (20.0%) quarterly, 9 (18.0%) every school term, 3 (6.0%) twice a year and 3 (6.0%) weekly or daily, as Figure 47 shows. A further 18 facilities (3.6%) described routine or scheduled servicing without a set interval, mostly scheduled visits by regional referral hospital maintenance teams, and 61 (12.3%) repaired items as the need arose. Ngwedo Seed Secondary School in Buliisa engaged a caretaker every month and used the Directorate of Industrial Training for furniture repairs, while Busaale reviewed asset condition every quarter.
Figure 47: Annual, monthly and quarterly checks were the most common stated intervals
Figure 47: Annual, monthly and quarterly checks were the most common stated intervals

Records. Of the 463 facilities that answered, 318 (68.7%) kept a regular record of asset functionality or breakdowns, 36 (7.8%) kept a partial or informal record, 80 (17.3%) kept none and 29 (6.3%) had not yet started because the assets were new or the facility was not yet operating. Of the 478 facilities that answered, 355 (74.3%) held a record of the UgIFT assets they received, 40 (8.4%) held a partial record, such as delivery notes only or a general register that does not identify UgIFT items, and 83 (17.4%) held none. Kagumba Health Centre III in Kamuli kept an asset condition book, a simple practice that other facilities can adopt.
4.2 Obsolete and Unserviceable Assets

Two wall-mounted aneroid blood-pressure machines at Nyanja Health Centre III, UGIFT-012842 and UGIFT-012843, were reported as spoilt, beyond repair and requiring replacement. Disposal approval or completion has not been confirmed.
